cards.title: One name, many answers
cards.body:
So far, [[DNS]] has turned a name into an address. But a domain like example.com needs more than one answer. There's the website's [[IPv4]] address, its [[IPv6]] address, and somewhere for email to go.

DNS keeps each kind of answer in a different **record**. When you look something up, you ask for a particular **record type**.

cards.title: Four record types
cards.body:
- An **A** record holds an **IPv4** address, like `198.51.100.10`. (A is for address.)
- An **AAAA** record holds an **IPv6** address, like `2001:db8::10`. It's called *quad-A* because an IPv6 address is four times as long as an IPv4 one: 128 [[bits|bit]] instead of 32.
- A **CNAME** record says "this name is an alias: go and look up this *other* name instead". For example, `www.example.com` can point to `example.com`.
- An **MX** record (mail exchange) names the [[server]] that receives **email** for the domain, with a priority number, like `10 mail.example.com`. If there are several, the **lowest** number is tried first.

cards.prompt: Match each record type to a value it could hold for example.com.
cards.explanation: **A** holds an IPv4 address (dots), and **AAAA** holds an IPv6 address (colons and [[hex]]). **CNAME** holds another *name* to look up instead. **MX** holds a priority number and the name of a mail server.
cards.hint: Look at the shape of each value: dots, colons, a plain name, or a number followed by a name.
cards.nudge: Dots mean [[IPv4]] and colons mean [[IPv6]]. One record holds just another name, and one holds a priority number plus a [[server]] name.

cards.prompt: An [[IPv6]] address is 128 [[bits|bit]] and an [[IPv4]] address is 32 bits. How many times longer is the IPv6 address?
cards.explanation: 128 ÷ 32 = **4**. That's where the name AAAA comes from: four times the length of an A record's address.
cards.hint: Divide the number of bits in an IPv6 address by the number in an IPv4 address.
cards.nudge: The question asks how many times longer, so divide the bigger bit count by the smaller one, rather than subtracting.

cards.prompt: Ask [[DNS]] for example.com's **AAAA** record by running `nslookup -type=AAAA example.com`.
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.output:
Server:		127.0.0.53
Address:	127.0.0.53#53

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:	example.com
Address: 2001:db8::10

cards.explanation: The answer is `2001:db8::10`, an [[IPv6]] address, because AAAA records hold IPv6 addresses. The address on the `Address:` line near the top, `127.0.0.53`, belongs to the DNS helper on this computer that answered the question, not to example.com.
cards.hint: Run the [[command]] from the prompt, then look below `Non-authoritative answer:` for the `Address:` line that belongs to example.com.
cards.nudge: The `Address:` near the top is the DNS helper that answered. You want the one after `Name: example.com`.

cards.prompt: Someone sends an email to `hello@example.com`. Which record type tells their mail [[server]] where to deliver it?

options.nudge: An A record gives an IPv4 address, often for the website. Email has a record type of its own.
AAAA gives an IPv6 address. Email has its own record type that names the mail server.
A CNAME just says "look up this other name instead". Which record names the server that receives email?

cards.explanation: **MX** (mail exchange) records name the server that receives email for a domain. The website and the mail server are often different machines, which is why email has its own record type. A and AAAA give addresses, and CNAME points to another name.
cards.hint: Only one record type is about email. Think back to what its name stands for.

cards.prompt: Run `dig www.example.com` and look at the ANSWER SECTION. There are two lines this time.
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: Look up www.example.com and show the full answer
commands.output:
; <<>> DiG 9.18.28 <<>> www.example.com
;; global options: +cmd
;; Got answer:
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 5170
;; flags: qr rd ra; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 2, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 1

;; OPT PSEUDOSECTION:
; EDNS: version: 0, flags:; udp: 65494
;; QUESTION SECTION:
;www.example.com.		IN	A

;; ANSWER SECTION:
www.example.com.	1800	IN	CNAME	example.com.
example.com.		1800	IN	A	198.51.100.10

;; Query time: 31 msec
;; SERVER: 127.0.0.53#53(127.0.0.53) (UDP)
;; WHEN: Tue Sep 29 10:16:40 UTC 2026
;; MSG SIZE  rcvd: 74

success.question: www.example.com is an alias for which name?

cards.explanation: The first line is a **CNAME** record: `www.example.com` is an alias for `example.com`. The [[resolver]] followed it and looked up example.com's **A** record on the second line, giving `198.51.100.10`. The dot at the end of `example.com.` is the root, from the first [[DNS]] lesson.
cards.hint: Run `dig www.example.com` and look at the first line of the ANSWER SECTION. The name at the end of that line is what it points to.
cards.nudge: Check the line with `CNAME` in it, not the one with `A`. The alias target is the last thing on that line, not an address.

cards.prompt: Put the steps in order for a [[browser]] opening `www.example.com`.

items.label: Get a CNAME record: it's an alias for example.com
Look up the A record for example.com

cards.explanation: A CNAME doesn't contain an address, just another name. So the lookup continues with **example.com** until it reaches an **A** record with an actual address. Only then can the browser connect.
cards.hint: A CNAME holds a name, not an address. You can't connect until you've got a real address.
cards.nudge: Each look-up comes before its answer, and connecting needs an actual address. What does the alias make the lookup do next?

cards.prompt: A message says "Log in to your example.com account" and offers four links. Which one really belongs to **example.com**?

options.nudge: Look closely at every character. One of them isn't the letter it seems to be, which makes it a different domain.
It starts with the right words, but what does it end with? The right-hand end decides who owns it.
A hyphen makes a new name, and this one ends with a different domain. Read from the right.

cards.explanation:
Read from the right. `login.example.com` ends in **example.com**, so it's a [[subdomain]] that example.com's owner controls.

- `examp1e.com` uses the digit **1** instead of the letter **l**. It's a completely different domain that anyone could register.
- The other two end in **example.org**, so they belong to whoever owns example.org, whatever the start of the name says.

Scammers register lookalike names like these to trick people into typing their passwords. Always check the right-hand end of the name.
cards.hint: Check the right-hand end of each name, letter by letter. The owner of that end controls the whole name.

cards.prompt: example.com has two [[MX records|mx-record]]: `10 mail.example.com` and `20 backup.example.com`. Which **priority number** does a sending mail [[server]] try first?
cards.explanation: With MX records, the **lower** number is tried first, so the priority **10** server, mail.example.com, gets the email. If it doesn't answer, the sender tries priority 20, the backup. It's like a to-do list: number 10 comes before number 20.
cards.hint: The record types card says which MX priority number is tried first when there are several. Look back at the MX line.
cards.nudge: Look back at the record types card: MX priority has its own rule about which number goes first. Type just the priority number, not the server name.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- [[DNS]] stores different kinds of answer in **records**.
- **A**: an [[IPv4]] address. **AAAA**: an [[IPv6]] address. **CNAME**: an alias for another name. **MX**: the mail server, with a priority (lower is tried first).
- `nslookup` and `dig` let you ask DNS questions yourself.
- Watch out for **lookalike** names: always check the right-hand end.

That's the end of the DNS lessons. Take the quiz to unlock [[Ports|port]] and [[Protocols|protocol]].
